_meta.description: Per-material SKIN-CONTACT safety floor for FDM parts worn or handled against intact skin (rings, bands, grips, earbud shells, jewelry, glasses, masks). Advisory RISK-STRATIFICATION, never certification: no 3D-printed part is skin-safe, hypoallergenic, or biocompatible. This public file is the always-free safety floor (honesty note + named hazards + the refer-to-medical boundary) so the caution reaches every install, offline included. Per-exposure verdicts, the remediation playbook, and the regulated-market compliance mapping are Kiln Pro/Business/Enterprise.
_meta._split_note: Safety floor only. The per-exposure verdict, remediation depth (which standard applies, what test answers it, sealing / cleanability), and the REACH / toy-safety compliance layer are curated in Kiln Pro. See https://kiln3d.com/pricing.
_meta.prime_directive: There is NO affirmative skin-safe verdict. 'No data' is returned as caution, never as safety. Out-of-scope uses (mouth/eye/mucosal, broken skin, piercing, implant, children's mouthing) are out of scope for a printed part — refer to a medical professional and a certified medical-grade material.

exposure_tiers.incidental: surface / intact skin, limited (<=24h) — brief handling
exposure_tiers.prolonged: surface / intact skin, prolonged (>24h) — worn items
exposure_tiers.mucosal: mucosal membrane — out of intact-skin scope
exposure_tiers.broken_implant: breached surface / implant / permanent — out of scope

family_inheritance._why: A worn part must never be met with SILENCE. A material with no record of its own used to return nothing, and nothing reads as 'no concern' — the opposite of the truth, which is 'untested'. An unmatched grade now inherits the closest characterised family and is labelled as inherited, so the caution reaches the user without ever being passed off as a record for their exact grade.
family_inheritance._direction: Inheritance resolves to the MOST RESTRICTIVE candidate, never the most convenient. In a filled grade the FILLER is usually the hazard, so a carbon-filled PLA inherits the fibre record, not plain PLA's. Resolving to the unfilled base would understate the risk, which is the one direction a safety floor must never fail in.

uncharacterized_floor._why: The last resort, and the reason silence is now impossible: a material we have never characterised still gets the honest floor. This is NOT a clearance — it is the statement that nobody has tested it, which is the most common truth in this domain.
uncharacterized_floor.concern_basis: no skin-contact record for this material — untested, which is not the same as low-risk

safety_floor.honesty_note: Kiln has no skin-contact record for this material. That is not a clearance: it means nobody has characterised it for wear against skin, and no 3D-printed part is skin-safe, hypoallergenic, or biocompatible in any case. Treat prolonged wear as unevaluated, and prefer a material Kiln does characterise for anything worn all day.

safety_floor.honesty_note: PVA is a water-soluble support material; sweat will turn a worn PVA part gummy, so it is simply the wrong material to wear. That is a fitness-for-use fact, not a toxicology verdict.

peek.concern_basis: certified grades are industrial-only; refer out

safety_floor.honesty_note: Implant-grade PEEK and medical PEI (ULTEM) are genuinely biocompatible, but that certification belongs to a qualified industrial material + process, not to anything a consumer desktop printer produces; do not treat it as a consumer skin-contact fix.

pvb.concern_basis: dissolved by the alcohol used to clean and sanitise a worn part — unsuitable before toxicology is even reached

safety_floor.honesty_note: PVB is the wrong material for anything worn, and the reason is upstream of toxicology. Its own resin maker specifies it as a 10% solution in aqueous ethanol at 20 C, and IPA smoothing is the filament's advertised feature — so hand sanitiser, alcohol wipes and sweat attack the part under exactly the conditions of wear. No skin assessment of the intact part would describe the part a wearer actually ends up with.

the filament maker's own SDS advises avoiding prolonged and repeated skin contact

pc_abs.concern_basis: dual-parent residual load — bisphenol A and phenolics from the PC phase, styrene and acrylonitrile from the ABS phase, all manufacturer-declared for the blend itself

safety_floor.honesty_note: PC-ABS carries both parents' chemistry, and this is not an inference: the manufacturer's own SDS names bisphenol A, styrene and acrylonitrile as residues of the blend. What is NOT known is whether any of it reaches skin — every migration dataset that exists is food-simulant, beverage or saliva, and none is sweat — so the concern is declared composition, never a measured skin dose.

pla_esd.concern_basis: a conductive carbon filler of undisclosed identity, on top of PLA's own undisclosed colorant load

safety_floor.honesty_note: PLA's benign reputation belongs to characterised medical-grade resin, and it does not extend to a carbon-loaded dissipative compound. A dissipative grade is its base polymer plus a conductive carbon whose identity the vendor usually withholds. The published hazard record for that carbon is inhalation-based, drawn from free powder rather than a printed part worn against skin, and no maker publishes skin testing for these grades — so the skin risk of an ESD part is not established as low, it is unmeasured.
